name: Schwab Total Stock Market Index Fund
strategy: Tracks the Dow Jones US Total Stock Market Index — about 3,400 stocks covering the full US market.
best_for: Total-market indexing for investors whose home base is Schwab
editorial: SWTSX completes the holy trinity of total-market funds — VTSAX, FZROX, SWTSX — and like its siblings it makes the case that this product category is finished evolving: the whole US market, 0.03%, no minimum, tracking error you'd need a magnifying glass to find. Schwab was a discount pioneer before index funds were cool, and this fund is that heritage distilled.

Choosing among the big three total-market funds is purely a question of where you bank: the funds are interchangeable, transaction fees apply if you buy one family's mutual funds at another's brokerage, and no rational person should pay a transaction fee to get 0.03% instead of 0.04%. One Schwab-specific note: it pays distributions annually rather than quarterly, a minor cash-drag quirk that matters less than almost anything else about your plan.

name: Schwab S&P 500 Index Fund
strategy: Tracks the S&P 500 index of 500 large US companies.
best_for: S&P 500 exposure at Schwab with a $0 minimum
editorial: Two basis points, no minimum, the S&P 500. SWPPX has quietly been one of the cheapest S&P 500 funds in existence for years, and it's a fine illustration of how completely the index price war has been won on behalf of ordinary savers: a fee this size on $100,000 is twenty dollars a year, less than the gas to drive to a financial advisor's office.

The fund-picking decision here is solved; the remaining decisions are human. An S&P 500 fund is 500 large companies, not the whole market and not a diversified portfolio by itself — pair it with international and bonds, or just confirm you're comfortable with a US-mega-cap-only equity base. Plenty of fortunes have been built on exactly that base; just choose it on purpose.

name: Schwab International Index Fund
strategy: Tracks the MSCI EAFE Index — large and mid-cap developed-market stocks outside North America.
best_for: Developed-international exposure in a Schwab three-fund portfolio
editorial: SWISX is Schwab's house international fund, and the key thing to know is what it leaves out: tracking MSCI EAFE means developed markets only — no emerging markets, and (EAFE quirk) no Canada. Around 700 stocks from Japan, Europe, and Australia at 0.06%. For Schwab loyalists building a three-fund portfolio, it's the standard international piece.

If you want emerging markets included, Schwab doesn't offer a total-international index mutual fund the way Vanguard (VTIAX) and Fidelity (FTIHX) do — the usual Schwab solutions are adding the ETF SCHE for emerging markets or simply using a competitor's total-international fund in an IRA elsewhere. None of this is disqualifying; it's just a lineup gap worth knowing before assuming SWISX equals 'everything outside the US.'

name: Schwab US Aggregate Bond Index Fund
strategy: Tracks the Bloomberg US Aggregate Bond Index — broad investment-grade US bonds.
best_for: The bond leg of a Schwab-based portfolio
editorial: Same Agg, different sticker: SWAGX tracks the identical Bloomberg US Aggregate index as VBTLX and FXNAX, at 0.04% with no minimum. Thousands of Treasuries, agency mortgage bonds, and investment-grade corporates with intermediate duration — the textbook ballast allocation, indexed without commentary.

Bond index funds are even more commoditized than stock index funds, because bonds themselves are math: yield, duration, credit quality. There is no secret sauce to differentiate one Agg tracker from another beyond a basis point of fee and a rounding error of tracking. Hold the one your brokerage sells without a transaction fee, put it in a tax-advantaged account, and spend your remaining attention on the stock/bond split — the only bond decision that moves the needle.

name: Schwab Small-Cap Index Fund
strategy: Tracks the Russell 2000 Index — 2,000 small US companies.
best_for: A cheap Russell 2000 sleeve at Schwab
editorial: SWSSX gives Schwab investors the Russell 2000 for 0.04% — small companies, big volatility, and the perennial academic promise of a size premium that shows up on its own erratic schedule. It's functionally interchangeable with Fidelity's FSSNX; both track the same index for almost the same nothing.

Small-cap funds reward a specific temperament: the willingness to watch your tilt lag the S&P 500 for five straight years without abandoning it, because the segment's outperformance historically arrives in violent, unannounced bursts. If you have that temperament, a few percent here is a reasonable lean. If you'll check the comparison chart quarterly and wince, SWTSX already owns these companies at market weight and will spare you the suspense.

name: Schwab 1000 Index Fund
strategy: Tracks the Schwab 1000 Index — the 1,000 largest US companies, roughly the S&P 500 plus mid caps.
best_for: Large-plus-mid-cap coverage in one proprietary index
editorial: The Schwab 1000 is Chuck Schwab's 1991 answer to index licensing fees — decades before Fidelity's ZERO funds made the same move famous. One thousand largest US companies, which lands the portfolio between an S&P 500 fund and a total-market fund: all the giants plus the mid caps, missing only the small-cap tail.

It's a perfectly good core fund with a 30-year record of doing exactly what it says, though in 2026 it occupies an awkward middle seat: SWPPX is cheaper for large-cap purists and SWTSX is more complete for two extra basis points. Long-time holders in taxable accounts have no reason to move; new money usually picks one of its more famous neighbors.

name: Schwab US Large-Cap Growth Index Fund
strategy: Tracks the Russell 1000 Growth Index — large US growth companies.
best_for: Indexed growth-style exposure on the Schwab platform
editorial: SWLGX is Schwab's entry in the cheap-growth-index category, tracking the same Russell 1000 Growth as Fidelity's FSPGX at the same 0.035%. The portfolio is what growth indexes always are now: a mega-cap tech core with everything else as garnish, concentrated enough that the top ten names drive most of the outcome.

The use case and the warning are identical to its Fidelity twin. Use case: getting growth-style exposure for thirty-five basis points less than the average active growth manager charges to underperform it. Warning: your total-market fund is already one-third these exact stocks, so a growth fund is a concentration dial, not a diversifier — turn it knowingly or not at all.

name: Schwab Target 2040 Index Fund
strategy: All-index target-date fund de-risking toward 2040, built from Schwab index funds and ETFs.
best_for: One-fund retirement investing at Schwab with a $1 minimum
editorial: Schwab's Target Index series is the least famous of the big three all-index target-date lineups and arguably the friendliest: 0.08% — matching Vanguard, undercutting Fidelity's Freedom Index — with a $1 minimum that makes the 'I don't have enough to start' excuse extinct. The 2040 fund currently runs equity-heavy and walks down the standard glide path.

As with all of these series, the construction differences (Schwab uses some of its own ETFs inside, glide paths differ by a few percentage points at various ages) are real but minor, and the deciding factor is where your accounts live. The headline is that a saver at any of the three big retail brokerages can now own a complete, self-managing, all-index retirement portfolio for eight to twelve basis points. That sentence took fifty years of fee wars to become true.

name: Schwab Target 2050 Index Fund
strategy: All-index target-date fund de-risking toward 2050; currently ~90% global equities.
best_for: Schwab savers a quarter-century from retirement
editorial: Ninety percent global stocks, ten percent bonds, rebalance forever, fade to conservative in the 2040s: SWYMX runs the standard 2050 playbook at Vanguard pricing with a one-dollar minimum. For a Schwab 401(k) or IRA, it's the complete answer in one ticker.

The under-discussed virtue of target-date funds shows up in the research on investor behavior: target-date owners' actual realized returns track their funds' returns far more closely than self-directed investors', whose buying-high-selling-low gap costs them 1–2% annually. The glide path gets the marketing attention, but the handcuffs are the product. SWYMX's are as comfortable and cheap as any.

name: Schwab Target 2060 Index Fund
strategy: All-index target-date fund de-risking toward 2060; currently ~90% global equities for the long haul.
best_for: Young Schwab investors who want to start with literally one dollar
editorial: A complete global portfolio, professionally maintained for forty years, for eight basis points and a one-dollar opening bid — SWYNX is a strong nominee for the lowest-barrier serious investment in America. The far-dated allocation is the usual ~90% world equity, and like all far-dated funds it won't meaningfully change for a decade-plus.

For a new investor choosing among the 2060 funds, here's the entire decision tree: Where are your accounts? Use that family's index target-date series. Is the word 'Index' in the fund name (Fidelity's trap)? Good. Now automate a contribution and close the tab. Everything else — Schwab vs. Vanguard glide-path nuance, eight versus twelve basis points — is hobbyist material, and this fund's owners have wisely chosen not to have this hobby.
